input.question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?
input.ground_truth: Followup question, my last name is August and I can trace myself back to Lithuania as "Augustinavicious" (anglicized). Would there be any connections between Augustus and Augustinavicious? My personal guess is "august" being a loanword, but I'm amazed it made it's way to Lithuania.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a friend named “Lucas.” Sometimes, when people from other countries talk about your friend, they might say “Lucas” or sometimes “Lucas’s” if they’re talking about something that belongs to him. But in English, we usually just say “Lucas.”

Long ago, people in Rome had names like “Hadrianus” or “Marcus.” When people in England started talking about these Roman emperors, they changed the names a little to make them easier to say in English. So “Hadrianus” became “Hadrian.” That’s called “anglicizing” the name.

But sometimes, they kept the names just like they were, like “Marcus.” It depends on how the name sounded and how English people liked to say it.

Now, about “Tit” and “August”—some Roman names are short, like “Titus.” But when we talk about Roman emperors, we usually use their full names or the ones that people used most. “Titus” is the full name, not just “Tit.” And “Augustus” is a special title that means “the revered one,” like a fancy way of saying “the great emperor.” So we don’t just call him “August,” we say “Augustus.”

So, people changed some names to make them easier to say in English, and some names stayed the same because that’s how everyone used them. And we use the full names or special titles for emperors, not just a part of their names.
